title: Grade 1 daily reading
overview: An adult reads authentic poems, fables, fantasy, legends, and historical nature prose across 180 evenings. Children respond orally, join refrains in shared readings, and revisit exact words. Suggested 10–15-minute sessions include rereading and three text-specific conversations; they do not assume independent decoding of historical vocabulary. The year moves from noticing patterns to remembering longer arcs, distinguishing observation from invention, and supporting interpretations. Historical myths and legends are identified as stories, and the nature excerpts distinguish figurative language and dated terminology from observation.

progression.focus: Hear patterns, notice details, and retell a short sequence.
progression.rationale: Adult reading and rereading make authentic verse, fables, and tales available while children join refrains, connect two events, and point to a spoken phrase.

progression.focus: Connect choices to consequences and compare different helpers.
progression.rationale: Longer linked scenes ask listeners to remember an earlier problem and distinguish what each character contributes. An adult recaps and rereads evidence.

progression.focus: Follow a continuing adventure and explain changes in a character.
progression.rationale: Several consecutive excerpts preserve the story’s arc. Children increasingly select details to explain a guess, while poems interrupt longer narrative runs.

progression.focus: Distinguish an imaginative explanation from an observation.
progression.rationale: Nature prose and literary myths invite questions about what can be observed and what the writer invents, without treating historical science as current authority.

progression.focus: Hear different voices and consider more than one interpretation.
progression.rationale: Dialogue, religious legend, and comic adventures stretch memory and inference. Discussion accepts differing readings when the child can connect them to words in the text.

progression.focus: Support an interpretation and connect form with meaning.
progression.rationale: Children take more initiative in finding a telling detail, comparing a beginning with an ending, or explaining how repetition or a narrator’s choice shapes a response. Adults still carry the reading load.

days.title: Johnny Crow’s Garden
days.challenge: Join the repeated garden refrain while remembering the animals’ different actions.
days.focus: Rhyming animal visitors and the change from confinement to a shared dinner.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.
days.contentNote: This playful historical verse mentions stocks, an old restraint used as punishment. Explain the word briefly; the guests are immediately released. It is fantasy, not information about animals.

excerpt.locator: Johnny Crow’s Garden; begins "JOHNNY CROW'S GARDEN."; ends '"GOOD-BYE!"'. Source block range 13–57 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: JOHNNY CROW'S GARDEN.

Johnny Crow
Would dig and sow
Till he made a little Garden.
And the Lion
Had a green and yellow Tie on
In Johnny Crow's Garden.

And the Rat
Wore a Feather in his Hat

But the Bear
Had nothing to wear
In Johnny Crow's Garden.
So the Ape
Took his Measure with a Tape
In Johnny Crow's Garden.
Then the Crane
Was caught in the Rain
In Johnny Crow's Garden.
And the Beaver
Was afraid he had a Fever
But the Goat
Said:
"It's nothing but his Throat!"
In Johnny Crow's Garden.

And the Pig
Danced a Jig
In Johnny Crow's Garden.

Then the Stork
Gave a Philosophic Talk

Till the Hippopotami
Said: "Ask no further 'What am I?'"

While the Elephant
Said something quite irrelevant
In Johnny Crow's Garden.

And the Goose--
Well,
the Goose was a Goose
In Johnny Crow's Garden.
And the Mouse
Built himself a little House
Where the Cat
Sat down beside the Mat
In Johnny Crow's Garden.
And the Whale
Told a very long Tale
In Johnny Crow's Garden.

And the Owl
Was a funny old Fowl
And the Fox
Put them all in the Stocks
In Johnny Crow's Garden.

But Johnny Crow
He let them go

And they all sat down
to their dinner in a row
In Johnny Crow's Garden.
"GOOD-BYE!"

questions.prompt: Which visitor needs clothes, and who begins helping?
facilitatorNotes: The Bear has nothing to wear; the Ape measures him. Ask how taking a measure could help make clothes.
evidence: Took his Measure with a Tape

questions.prompt: What makes the Whale’s activity fit its rhyming name?
facilitatorNotes: Whale pairs with Tale. Invite the child to hear how the rhyme turns a visitor into a tiny story.
evidence: Told a very long Tale

questions.prompt: How does Johnny change the Fox’s ending for the guests?
facilitatorNotes: The Fox puts them in stocks; Johnny releases them and everyone eats together. Discuss what the final gathering feels like.
evidence: He let them go

days.title: The Cock and the Pearl
days.challenge: Distinguish an object’s shine from its usefulness to a particular character.
days.focus: The fable’s contrast between food and treasure.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator: The Cock and the Pearl; begins 'The Cock and the Pearl'; ends 'Precious things are for those that can prize them.'. Source block range 35–37 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: The Cock and the Pearl

A cock was once strutting up and down the farmyard among the hens when suddenly he espied something shinning amid the straw. “Ho! ho!” quoth he, “that’s for me,” and soon rooted it out from beneath the straw. “What did it turn out to be but a Pearl that by some chance had been lost in the yard? “You may be a treasure,” quoth Master Cock, “to men that prize you, but for me I would rather have a single barley-corn than a peck of pearls.”
Precious things are for those that can prize them.

questions.prompt: What first makes the cock notice the pearl?
facilitatorNotes: Something shines among the straw; he roots it out before knowing its value.
evidence: shinning amid the straw

questions.prompt: Why does the cock prefer one grain to many pearls?
facilitatorNotes: Grain is food for him. The pearl may be valuable to people, but does not meet his need.
evidence: a single barley-corn than a peck of pearls

questions.prompt: Does the ending mean nobody can value a pearl?
facilitatorNotes: No. The cock says it is treasure to people who prize it. Ask how two people might value the same thing differently.
evidence: to men that prize you

blocks.text: DAFFODOWNDILLY

She wore her yellow sun-bonnet,
She wore her greenest gown;
She turned to the south wind
And curtsied up and down.
She turned to the sunlight
And shook her yellow head,
And whispered to her neighbour:
“Winter is dead.”

questions.prompt: What parts of the flower are imagined as clothes?
facilitatorNotes: A yellow sun-bonnet and green gown suggest flower and stem or leaves. Accept the child’s supported drawing or gesture.
evidence: her yellow sun-bonnet

questions.prompt: Which action makes the flower seem polite like a person?
facilitatorNotes: It curtsies. Connect bending up and down with a flower moving in the wind.
evidence: curtsied up and down

questions.prompt: What does Winter is dead mean in this flower poem?
facilitatorNotes: Winter has ended and spring has arrived; it is not about a person’s death. Ask which sunlight and flower details support this reading.
evidence: “Winter is dead.”

days.title: The Sugar-Plum Tree
days.challenge: Follow a fanciful cause-and-effect chain through four stanzas.
days.focus: A bedtime invitation uses impossible food images and a playful solution.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator:
The Sugar-Plum Tree; begins 'THE SUGAR-PLUM TREE'; ends 'loser to me
In your dainty white nightcap and gown,
And I’ll rock you away to that Sugar-Plum Tree
In the garden of Shut-Eye Town.'. Source block range 96–100 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: THE SUGAR-PLUM TREE

Have you ever heard of the Sugar-Plum Tree?
’Tis a marvel of great renown!
It blooms on the shore of the Lollipop sea
In the garden of Shut-Eye Town;
The fruit that it bears is so wondrously sweet
(As those who have tasted it say)
That good little children have only to eat
Of that fruit to be happy next day.

When you’ve got to the tree, you would have a hard time
To capture the fruit which I sing;
The tree is so tall that no person could climb
To the boughs where the sugar-plums swing!
But up in that tree sits a chocolate cat,
And a gingerbread dog prowls below—
And this is the way you contrive to get at
Those sugar-plums tempting you so:

You say but the word to that gingerbread dog
And he barks with such terrible zest
That the chocolate cat is at once all agog,
As her swelling proportions attest.
And the chocolate cat goes cavorting around
From this leafy limb unto that,
And the sugar-plums tumble, of course, to the ground—
Hurrah for that chocolate cat!

There are marshmallows, gumdrops, and peppermint canes,
With stripings of scarlet or gold,
And you carry away of the treasure that rains
As much as your apron can hold!
So come, little child, cuddle closer to me
In your dainty white nightcap and gown,
And I’ll rock you away to that Sugar-Plum Tree
In the garden of Shut-Eye Town.

questions.prompt: Why can the child not simply climb to the sugar-plums?
facilitatorNotes: The tree is too tall to climb to its boughs. This problem leads to the dog-and-cat plan.
evidence: The tree is so tall that no person could climb

questions.prompt: How does the gingerbread dog help the fruit reach the ground?
facilitatorNotes: Its barking excites the cat, which moves through the branches and shakes the sugar-plums down.
evidence: And the sugar-plums tumble, of course, to the ground

questions.prompt: Which ending words show this journey belongs to bedtime imagination?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker cuddles and rocks the child toward Shut-Eye Town. Discuss why a dream garden can contain candy creatures.
evidence: I’ll rock you away to that Sugar-Plum Tree

days.title: The Dog and the Shadow
days.challenge: Separate what the dog thinks he sees from what the narrator says is there.
days.focus: A mistaken reflection and the consequence of grasping for more.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator: The Dog and the Shadow; begins 'The Dog and the Shadow'; ends 'Beware lest you lose the substance by grasping at the shadow.'. Source block range 47–49 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: The Dog and the Shadow

It happened that a Dog had got a piece of meat and was carrying it home in his mouth to eat it in peace. Now on his way home he had to cross a plank lying across a running brook. As he crossed, he looked down and saw his own shadow reflected in the water beneath. Thinking it was another dog with another piece of meat, he made up his mind to have that also. So he made a snap at the shadow in the water, but as he opened his mouth the piece of meat fell out, dropped into the water and was never seen more.
Beware lest you lose the substance by grasping at the shadow.

questions.prompt: What is the other dog actually, according to the narrator?
facilitatorNotes: His own reflected image in the water. The story calls it a shadow reflected; use the text’s wording while clarifying reflection.
evidence: his own shadow reflected in the water beneath

questions.prompt: At what moment does he lose the real meat?
facilitatorNotes: When he opens his mouth to snap at the apparent second piece.
evidence: as he opened his mouth the piece of meat fell out

questions.prompt: What could the dog have checked before trying to take more?
facilitatorNotes: He could have noticed the image copying him or kept his own food. These are proposed alternatives, not events the story reports.
evidence: Thinking it was another dog

days.title: Spring Morning
days.challenge: Track a repeated question while imagining a change from ground-level to sky-level view.
days.focus: Freedom, movement, and surprising comparisons of sky and water.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

Spring Morning; begins 'SPRING MORNING'; ends 'n’t quite know.
What does it matter where people go?
Down to the wood where the blue-bells grow—
Anywhere, anywhere. I don’t know.'. Source block range 123–129 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: SPRING MORNING

Where am I going? I don’t quite know.
Down to the stream where the king-cups grow—
Up on the hill where the pine trees blow—
Anywhere, anywhere. I don’t know.

Where am I going? The clouds sail by,
Little ones, baby ones, over the sky.
Where am I going? The shadows pass,
Little ones, baby ones, over the grass.

If you were a cloud, and sailed up there,
You’d sail on water as blue as air,
And you’d see me here in the fields and say:
“Doesn’t the sky look green to-day?”

Where am I going? The high rooks call:
“It’s awful fun to be born at all.”
Where am I going? The ring-doves coo:
“We do have beautiful things to do.”

If you were a bird, and lived on high,
You’d lean on the wind when the wind came by,
You’d say to the wind when it took you away:
“That’s where I wanted to go to-day!”

Where am I going? I don’t quite know.
What does it matter where people go?
Down to the wood where the blue-bells grow—
Anywhere, anywhere. I don’t know.

questions.prompt: Name two places the speaker might go without making a fixed plan.
facilitatorNotes: The stream, hill, or wood fit the stated possibilities. Ask which sounds or plants make a place attractive.
evidence: Down to the stream where the king-cups grow

questions.prompt: Why could the imagined cloud call the sky green?
facilitatorNotes: From above, the green fields beneath can be imagined as its sky. Help the child reverse the usual viewpoint.
evidence: Doesn’t the sky look green to-day?

questions.prompt: Does I don’t quite know sound worried here or open to adventure?
facilitatorNotes: Open and curious fits the beautiful sights and Anywhere refrain. Accept a different feeling if supported by a particular line.
evidence: Anywhere, anywhere. I don’t know.

days.title: The Best Thing in the World — the first guesses
days.challenge: Remember how three characters give different meanings to the same phrase.
days.focus: A repeated announcement gathers a growing group of searchers.
days.context: Part 1 of a complete chapter read over three consecutive nights. Animal characters speak and reason like people; their preferences drive this fantasy.

excerpt.locator: The Best Thing in the World — the first guesses; begins 'OLD MOTHER WEST WIND had stopped to talk with the Slender Fir Tree.'; ends 'e could go after Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit, for there is nothing that Bobby Coon likes to eat so well as sweet milky corn.'. Source block range 347–357 in the documented transcription extraction. Dated 1914 witness printed pages 115–117.

blocks.text: OLD MOTHER WEST WIND had stopped to talk with the Slender Fir Tree.
“I’ve just come across the Green Meadows,” said Old Mother West Wind, “and there I saw the Best Thing in the World.”

Striped Chipmunk was sitting under the Slender Fir Tree and he couldn’t help hearing what Old Mother West Wind said. “The Best Thing in the World—now what can that be?” thought Striped Chipmunk. “Why it must be heaps and heaps of nuts and acorns! I’ll go and find it.”
So Striped Chipmunk started down the Lone Little Path through the wood as fast as he could run. Pretty soon he met Peter Rabbit.
“Where are you going in such a hurry, Striped Chipmunk?” asked Peter Rabbit.
“Down in the Green Meadows to find the Best Thing in the World,” replied Striped Chipmunk, and ran faster.
“The Best Thing in the World,” said Peter Rabbit, “why, that must be a great pile of carrots and cabbage! I think I’ll go and find it.”
So Peter Rabbit started down the Lone Little Path through the wood as fast as he could go after Striped Chipmunk.
As they passed the great hollow tree Bobby Coon put his head out. “Where are you going in such a hurry?” asked Bobby Coon.
“Down in the Green Meadows to find the Best Thing in the World!” shouted Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit, and both began to run faster.
“The Best Thing in the World,” said Bobby Coon to himself, “why, that must be a whole field of sweet milky corn. I think I’ll go and find it.”

So Bobby Coon climbed down out of the great hollow tree and started down the Lone Little Path through the wood as fast as he could go after Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit, for there is nothing that Bobby Coon likes to eat so well as sweet milky corn.

questions.prompt: What does Striped Chipmunk imagine the best thing will be?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines nuts and acorns; the announcement itself never names these.
evidence: heaps and heaps of nuts and acorns

questions.prompt: How is Peter Rabbit’s answer different?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines carrots and cabbage instead of nuts, showing his own preferences.
evidence: a great pile of carrots and cabbage

questions.prompt: What makes Bobby Coon join the search?
facilitatorNotes: Hearing the same exciting claim and imagining sweet corn. Ask whether anyone has checked these guesses yet.
evidence: a whole field of sweet milky corn

days.title: The Best Thing in the World — one neighbor stays
days.challenge: Compare the rushing group with the character who chooses not to join.
days.focus: Johnny Chuck offers a different kind of answer to the repeated question.
days.context: Part 2. Chipmunk, Rabbit, and Coon are searching for the Best Thing, each imagining a favorite food. More neighbors hear about the search.

excerpt.locator: The Best Thing in the World — one neighbor stays; begins 'At the edge of the wood they met Jimmy Skunk. “Where are you going in such a hurry?” asked Jimmy Sku'; ends 'd at home and played all day among the flowers with the Merry Little Breezes of Old Mother West Wind and was as happy as could be.'. Source block range 358–370 in the documented transcription extraction. Dated 1914 witness printed pages 117–119.

blocks.text: At the edge of the wood they met Jimmy Skunk. “Where are you going in such a hurry?” asked Jimmy Skunk.
“Down in the Green Meadows to find the Best Thing in the World!” shouted Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit and Bobby Coon. Then they all tried to run faster.

“The Best Thing in the World,” said Jimmy Skunk. “Why, that must be packs and packs of beetles!” And for once in his life Jimmy Skunk began to hurry down the Lone Little Path after Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit and Bobby Coon.
They were all running so fast that they didn’t see Reddy Fox until he jumped out of the long grass and asked:
“Where are you going in such a hurry?”
“To find the Best Thing in the World!” shouted Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit and Bobby Coon and Jimmy Skunk, and each did his best to run faster.
“The Best Thing in the World,” said Reddy Fox to himself. “Why, that must be a whole pen full of tender young chickens, and I must have them.”
So away went Reddy Fox as fast as he could run down the Lone Little Path after Striped Chipmunk, Peter Rabbit, Bobby Coon, and Jimmy Skunk.
By and by they all came to the house of Johnny Chuck.
“Where are you going in such a hurry?” asked Johnny Chuck.
“To find the Best Thing in the World,” shouted Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit and Bobby Coon and Jimmy Skunk and Reddy Fox.
“The Best Thing in the World,” said Johnny Chuck. “Why, I don’t know of anything better than my own little home and the warm sunshine and the beautiful blue sky.”
So Johnny Chuck stayed at home and played all day among the flowers with the Merry Little Breezes of Old Mother West Wind and was as happy as could be.

questions.prompt: What does Jimmy Skunk’s unusual hurry tell us about his wish?
facilitatorNotes: He wants the imagined beetles enough to hurry despite his usual pace. Keep the inference tied to for once.
evidence: for once in his life Jimmy Skunk began to hurry

questions.prompt: What three things does Johnny already enjoy?
facilitatorNotes: His home, warm sunshine, and blue sky. Unlike the others, he names things present around him.
evidence: my own little home and the warm sunshine and the beautiful blue sky

questions.prompt: How does Johnny spend the day instead of running?
facilitatorNotes: He plays among flowers with the Breezes and feels happy. Discuss whether staying is laziness or contentment in this scene.
evidence: was as happy as could be

days.title: The Best Thing in the World — what the search misses
days.challenge: Use the group’s ending condition to reconsider its starting expectations.
days.focus: An explicit fable-like conclusion names contentment after showing its opposite.
days.context: Part 3 and the end of the chapter. Johnny stayed home happily while the other animals searched all day.

excerpt.locator: The Best Thing in the World — what the search misses; begins 'But all day long Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit and Bobby Coon and Jimmy Skunk and Reddy Fox ran '; ends 'Wind. “It is being happy with the things you have and not wanting things which some one else has. And it is called Con-tent-ment.”'. Source block range 371–375 in the documented transcription extraction. Dated 1914 witness printed pages 119–120.

blocks.text: But all day long Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit and Bobby Coon and Jimmy Skunk and Reddy Fox ran this way and ran that way over the Green Meadows trying to find the Best Thing in the World. The sun was very, very warm and they ran so far and they ran so fast that they were very, very hot and tired, and still they hadn’t found the Best Thing in the World.

When the long day was over they started up the Lone Little Path past Johnny Chuck’s house to their own homes. They didn’t hurry now for they were so very, very tired! And they were cross—oh, so cross! Striped Chipmunk hadn’t found a single nut. Peter Rabbit hadn’t found so much as the leaf of a cabbage. Bobby Coon hadn’t found the tiniest bit of sweet milky corn. Jimmy Skunk hadn’t seen a single beetle. Reddy Fox hadn’t heard so much as the peep of a chicken. And all were as hungry as hungry could be.
Half way up the Lone Little Path they met Old Mother West Wind going to her home behind the hill. “Did you find the Best Thing in the World?” asked Old Mother West Wind.
“No!” shouted Striped Chipmunk and Peter Rabbit and Bobby Coon and Jimmy Skunk and Reddy Fox all together.
“Johnny Chuck has it,” said Old Mother West Wind. “It is being happy with the things you have and not wanting things which some one else has. And it is called Con-tent-ment.”

questions.prompt: How do the searchers feel when the day is over?
facilitatorNotes: Hot, tired, cross, and hungry; their fast search has not supplied any imagined food.
evidence: And all were as hungry as hungry could be

questions.prompt: What has Johnny found without making the search?
facilitatorNotes: Contentment, happiness with what he has. Invite the child to connect this with his home and outdoor play from the preceding scene.
evidence: Johnny Chuck has it

questions.prompt: Does this story prove that wanting any new thing is always wrong?
facilitatorNotes: No. Its particular warning concerns the unhappy chase after imagined things. A child can discuss a useful goal that differs from this frantic search.
evidence: being happy with the things you have

days.title: Wynken, Blynken, and Nod
days.challenge: Hold an imagined voyage in mind until the final stanza reveals a bedtime meaning.
days.focus: A lullaby transforms eyes, a head, and a bed into fishermen and a boat.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator:
Wynken, Blynken, and Nod; begins 'WYNKEN, BLYNKEN, AND NOD'; ends 'll see the beautiful things
As you rock in the misty sea,
Where the old shoe rocked the fishermen three:
Wynken,
Blynken,
And Nod.'. Source block range 192–196 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: WYNKEN, BLYNKEN, AND NOD

Wynken, Blynken, and Nod one night
Sailed off in a wooden shoe—
Sailed on a river of crystal light,
Into a sea of dew.
“Where are you going, and what do you wish?”
The old moon asked the three.
“We have come to fish for the herring fish
That live in this beautiful sea;
Nets of silver and gold have we!”
Said Wynken,
Blynken,
And Nod.

The old moon laughed and sang a song,
As they rocked in the wooden shoe,
And the wind that sped them all night long
Ruffled the waves of dew.
The little stars were the herring fish
That lived in that beautiful sea—
“Now cast your nets wherever you wish—
Never afeard are we”;
So cried the stars to the fishermen three:
Wynken,
Blynken,
And Nod.

All night long their nets they threw
To the stars in the twinkling foam—
Then down from the skies came the wooden shoe,
Bringing the fishermen home;
’Twas all so pretty a sail it seemed
As if it could not be,
And some folks thought ’twas a dream they’d dreamed
Of sailing that beautiful sea—
But I shall name you the fishermen three:
Wynken,
Blynken,
And Nod.

Wynken and Blynken are two little eyes,
And Nod is a little head,
And the wooden shoe that sailed the skies
Is a wee one’s trundle-bed.
So shut your eyes while mother sings
Of wonderful sights that be,
And you shall see the beautiful things
As you rock in the misty sea,
Where the old shoe rocked the fishermen three:
Wynken,
Blynken,
And Nod.

questions.prompt: What do the travelers use instead of an ordinary boat?
facilitatorNotes: A wooden shoe. Invite the child to describe how this impossible boat prepares us for dream travel.
evidence: Sailed off in a wooden shoe

questions.prompt: What are the herring fish in this imagined sea?
facilitatorNotes: The little stars. The poem makes the sky into water and stars into a catch.
evidence: The little stars were the herring fish

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza change our understanding of the three names?
facilitatorNotes: Wynken and Blynken become eyes and Nod a head; the voyage connects to falling asleep.
evidence: Wynken and Blynken are two little eyes

days.title: The Story of the First Butterflies
days.challenge: Follow a beautiful object’s transformation while distinguishing a myth from an observation.
days.focus: A historical literary adaptation links butterfly colors with shining stones.
days.context: Holbrook’s 1902 English adaptation tells an imagined origin of butterflies. Discuss its colors and care for children as literature, not a scientific explanation or a verified account of one named Indigenous tradition.
days.contentNote: The collection uses a generalized Great Spirit figure without naming a source community here. Do not present the adaptation as what all Indigenous peoples believe.

excerpt.locator: The Story of the First Butterflies; begins 'THE STORY OF THE FIRST BUTTERFLIES.'; ends 'tiful thought of the Great Spirit, and in their wings were all the colors of the shining stones that he did not wish to hide away.'. Source block range 48–54 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: THE STORY OF THE FIRST BUTTERFLIES.

The Great Spirit thought, "By and by I will make men, but first I will make a home for them. It shall be very bright and beautiful. There shall be mountains and prairies and forests, and about it all shall be the blue waters of the sea."

As the Great Spirit had thought, so he did. He gave the earth a soft cloak of green. He made the prairies beautiful with flowers. The forests were bright with birds of many colors, and the sea was the home of wonderful sea-creatures. "My children will love the prairies, the forests, and the seas," he thought, "but the mountains look dark and cold. They are very dear to me, but how shall I make my children go to them and so learn to love them?"

Long the Great Spirit thought about the mountains. At last, he made many little shining stones. Some were red, some blue, some green, some yellow, and some were shining with all the lovely colors of the beautiful rainbow. "All my children will love what is beautiful," he thought, "and if I hide the bright stones in the seams of the rocks of the mountains, men will come to find them, and they will learn to love my mountains."

When the stones were made and the Great Spirit looked upon their beauty, he said, "I will not hide you all away in the seams of the rocks. Some of you shall be out in the sunshine, so that the little children who cannot go to the mountains shall see your colors." Then the southwind came by, and as he went, he sang softly of forests flecked with light and shadow, of birds and their nests in the leafy trees. He sang of long summer days and the music of waters beating upon the shore. He sang of the moonlight and the starlight. All the wonders of the night, all the beauty of the morning, were in his song.

"Dear southwind," said the Great Spirit "here are some beautiful things for you to bear away with, you to your summer home. You will love them, and all the little children will love them." At these words of the Great Spirit, all the stones before him stirred with life and lifted themselves on many-colored wings. They fluttered away in the sunshine, and the southwind sang to them as they went.
So it was that the first butterflies came from a beautiful thought of the Great Spirit, and in their wings were all the colors of the shining stones that he did not wish to hide away.

questions.prompt: Why are some bright stones hidden in the mountains in this story?
facilitatorNotes: The Great Spirit hopes their beauty will draw people to mountains they might otherwise avoid.
evidence: men will come to find them

questions.prompt: Why are other stones left in the sunshine?
facilitatorNotes: So children who cannot reach the mountains can enjoy their colors too.
evidence: the little children who cannot go to the mountains

questions.prompt: What changes the stones into butterflies, and is this a scientific account?
facilitatorNotes: At the Great Spirit’s words they move and gain wings. Name it as the story’s imaginative explanation, not how butterflies actually develop.
evidence: lifted themselves on many-colored wings

days.title: Corner-of-the-Street
days.challenge: Notice how a tiny sound pattern can suggest people approaching.
days.focus: Footwear and repeated sounds make a short street scene lively.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

blocks.text: CORNER-OF-THE-STREET

Down by the corner of the street,
Where the three roads meet,
And the feet
Of the people as they pass go “Tweet-tweet-tweet—”
Who comes tripping round the corner of the street?
One pair of shoes which are Nurse’s;
One pair of slippers which are Percy’s . . .
Tweet! Tweet! Tweet!

questions.prompt: Where do the people’s paths meet?
facilitatorNotes: At a corner where three roads meet. A quick sketch can locate the corner without inventing a town.
evidence: Where the three roads meet

questions.prompt: What two kinds of footwear appear at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Nurse’s shoes and Percy’s slippers. Ask how those details let the poem introduce people through their feet.
evidence: One pair of slippers which are Percy’s

questions.prompt: What does Tweet-tweet-tweet make the walking sound like to you?
facilitatorNotes: It can suggest quick, light, musical steps. Accept other sound impressions grounded in the repeated syllables, not a literal unseen bird.
evidence: Tweet! Tweet! Tweet!

days.title: The Fox and the Mask
days.challenge: Notice how a closer look changes the fox’s first conclusion.
days.focus: A theatrical prop supports a distinction between appearance and inner qualities.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator: The Fox and the Mask; begins 'The Fox and the Mask'; ends 'Outside show is a poor substitute for inner worth.'. Source block range 106–108 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: The Fox and the Mask

A Fox had by some means got into the store-room of a theatre. Suddenly he observed a face glaring down on him and began to be very frightened; but looking more closely he found it was only a Mask such as actors use to put over their face. “Ah,” said the Fox, “you look very fine; it is a pity you have not got any brains.”
Outside show is a poor substitute for inner worth.

questions.prompt: Why is the fox frightened at first?
facilitatorNotes: He mistakes a mask for a glaring face. Ask what looking closer changes.
evidence: a face glaring down on him

questions.prompt: What is a mask in this particular story?
facilitatorNotes: An object actors wear over their faces, not a living head. The narrator explains this directly.
evidence: such as actors use to put over their face

questions.prompt: Why is the remark about brains a joke?
facilitatorNotes: A fine-looking mask cannot think. The final saying turns that literal fact into a comment about judging appearances.
evidence: Outside show is a poor substitute for inner worth.

days.title: The Wind’s Work
days.challenge: Remember several neighbors’ different needs for the same change in weather.
days.focus: Linked jobs and a recurring wish connect one child’s play with community work.
days.context: A historical story of a wind-powered town. The adult reads the complete story, excluding the separate teaching motto that precedes it. A footnote in the book says the Sea-captain’s song is sung to the tune of “Nancy Lee.”

excerpt.locator: The Wind’s Work; begins 'One morning Jan waked up very early, and the first thing he saw when he opened his eyes was his grea'; ends 'if it had wings; till it slipped away from the string, and Jan never saw it again, and only the wind knew where it landed at last.'. Source block range 30–50 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: One morning Jan waked up very early, and the first thing he saw when he opened his eyes was his great kite in the corner. His big brother had made it for him; and it had a smiling face, and a long tail that reached from the bed to the fireplace. It did not smile at Jan that morning though, but looked very sorrowful and seemed to say "Why was I made? Not to stand in a corner, I hope!" for it had been finished for two whole days and not a breeze had blown to carry it up like a bird in the air.

Jan jumped out of bed, dressed himself, and ran to the door to see if the windmill on the hill was at work; for he hoped that the wind had come in the night. But the mill was silent and its arms stood still. Not even a leaf turned over in the yard.

The windmill stood on a high hill where all the people could see it, and when its long arms went whirling around every one knew that there was no danger of being hungry, for then the Miller was busy from morn to night grinding the grain that the farmers brought him.
When Jan looked out, however, the Miller had nothing to do, and was standing in his doorway, watching the clouds, and saying to himself (though Jan could not hear him):—

"Oh! how I wish the wind would blow
So that my windmill's sails might go,
To turn my heavy millstones round!
For corn and wheat must both be ground,
And how to grind I do not know
Unless the merry wind will blow."
He sighed as he spoke, for he looked down in the village, and saw the Baker in neat cap and apron, standing idle too.
The Baker's ovens were cold, and his trays were clean, and he, too, was watching the sky, and saying:—

"Oh! how I wish the wind would blow,
So that the Miller's mill might go,
And grind me flour so fine, to make
My good light bread and good sweet cake!
But how to bake I do not know
Without the flour as white as snow."

Jan heard every word that the Baker said, for he lived next door to him; and he felt so sorry for his good neighbor that he wanted to tell him so. But before he had time to speak, somebody else called out from across the street:—

"Well! I'm sure I wish the wind would blow,
For this is washing day, you know.
I've scrubbed and rubbed with all my might,
In tubs of foam from morning light,
And now I want the wind to blow
To dry my clothes as white as snow."
This was the Washerwoman who was hanging out her clothes. Jan could see his own Sunday shirt, with ruffles, hanging limp on her line, and it was as white as a snowflake, sure enough!

"Come over, little neighbor," cried the Washerwoman, when she saw Jan. "Come over, little neighbor, and help me work to-day!" So, as soon as Jan had eaten his breakfast, he ran over to carry her basket for her. The basket was heavy, but he did not care; and as he worked he heard some one singing a song, with a voice almost as loud and as strong as the wind.

"Oh! if the merry wind would blow,
Yeo ho! lads, ho! yeo ho! yeo ho!
My gallant ship would gaily go,
Yeo ho! lads, ho! yeo ho!
In fresh'ning gales we'd loose our sails,
And o'er the sea,
Where blue waves dance, and sunbeams glance,
We'd sail in glee,
But winds must blow, before we go,
Across the sea,
Yeo ho! my lads, yeo ho!"

Jan and the Washerwoman and all the neighbors looked out to see who was singing so cheerily, and it was the Sea-captain whose white ship Jan had watched in the harbor. The ship was laden with linen and laces for fine ladies, but it could not go till the wind blew. The Captain was impatient to be off, and so he walked about town, singing his jolly song to keep himself happy.

Jan thought it was a beautiful song, and when he went home he tried to sing it himself. He did not know all the words, but he put his hands in his pockets and swelled out his little chest and sang in as big a voice as he could: "Yeo ho! my lads, yeo ho!"

While he sang, something kissed him on the cheek; and when he turned to see what it was his hat spun off into the yard as if it were enchanted; and when he ran to pick his hat up he heard a whispering all through the town. He looked up, and he looked down, and on every side, but saw nobody! At last the golden weather-vane on the church tower called down:—
"Foolish child, it is the wind from out of the east."
The trees had been the first to know of its coming, and they were bowing and bending to welcome it; while the leaves danced off the branches and down the hill, in a whirl of delight.

The windmill's arms whirled round, oh! so fast, and the wheat was ground into white flour for the Baker, who kindled his fires and beat his eggs in the twinkling of an eye; and he was not quicker than the Sea-captain, who loosed his sails in the fresh'ning gales, just as he had said he would, and sailed away to foreign lands.
Jan watched him go, and then ran in great haste to get his kite; for the petticoats on the Washerwoman's clothesline were puffed up like balloons, and all the world was astir.

"Now I'm in my proper place," said the kite as it sailed over the roofs of the houses, over the tree tops, over the golden weather vane, and even over the windmill itself. Higher, higher, higher it flew, as if it had wings; till it slipped away from the string, and Jan never saw it again, and only the wind knew where it landed at last.

questions.prompt: Why does the baker need something to happen at the mill first?
facilitatorNotes: The baker needs flour, and the mill needs wind to turn its sails and grind grain.
evidence: Without the flour as white as snow

questions.prompt: Which early detail shows Jan that there is no wind yet?
facilitatorNotes: The mill arms are still and no leaf turns over. These visible clues explain his disappointment.
evidence: Not even a leaf turned over in the yard.

questions.prompt: Does the arriving wind solve every wish exactly as Jan hopes?
facilitatorNotes: It starts the work and lifts his kite, but the kite escapes. Discuss the mixed ending instead of calling it simply happy or sad.
evidence: Jan never saw it again

days.title: Halfway Down
days.challenge: Follow contrasts between up/down and here/elsewhere in a small familiar place.
days.focus: A child gives an ordinary stair a private imaginative meaning.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator:
Halfway Down; begins 'HALFWAY DOWN'; ends '
It isn’t in the town.
And all sorts of funny thoughts
Run round my head:
“It isn’t really
Anywhere!
It’s somewhere else
Instead!”'. Source block range 226–228 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: HALFWAY DOWN

Halfway down the stairs
Is a stair
Where I sit.
There isn’t any
Other stair
Quite like
It.
I’m not at the bottom,
I’m not at the top;
So this is the stair
Where
I always
Stop.

Halfway up the stairs
Isn’t up,
And isn’t down.
It isn’t in the nursery,
It isn’t in the town.
And all sorts of funny thoughts
Run round my head:
“It isn’t really
Anywhere!
It’s somewhere else
Instead!”

questions.prompt: What makes the chosen stair different from the top or bottom?
facilitatorNotes: It is between them and is where the speaker always stops. Its importance is personal, not that it has a stated different shape.
evidence:
I’m not at the bottom,
I’m not at the top

questions.prompt: Why might the same place be called halfway down and halfway up?
facilitatorNotes: The description depends on which direction you imagine going. Both phrases can name the same middle place.
evidence: Halfway up the stairs

questions.prompt: Is the stair literally nowhere when the speaker says it isn’t really anywhere?
facilitatorNotes: No; the poem names the stair clearly. The ending describes an imaginative in-between place where thoughts wander.
evidence:
It’s somewhere else
Instead!

days.title: The Dinkey-Bird
days.challenge: Listen past unfamiliar musical words to follow the poem’s repeating place and mood.
days.focus: Invented names, candy plants, and song create a world of play.
days.context: An adult reads the musical words expressively; the child need not decode or define every technical term to hear the joyful pattern. Wonder-Wander and the amfalula tree are invented.

excerpt.locator:
The Dinkey-Bird; begins 'THE DINKEY-BIRD'; ends ' comprehend!
Speed, little dreams, your winging
To that land across the sea
Where the Dinkey-Bird is singing
In the amfalula tree!'. Source block range 358–364 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: THE DINKEY-BIRD

In an ocean, ’way out yonder
(As all sapient people know),
Is the land of Wonder-Wander,
Whither children love to go;
It’s their playing, romping, swinging,
That give great joy to me
While the Dinkey-Bird goes singing
In the amfalula tree!

There the gum-drops grow like cherries,
And taffy’s thick as peas—
Caramels you pick like berries
When, and where, and how you please;
Big red sugar-plums are clinging
To the cliffs beside that sea
Where the Dinkey-Bird is singing
In the amfalula tree.

So when children shout and scamper
And make merry all the day,
When there’s naught to put a damper
To the ardor of their play;
When I hear their laughter ringing,
Then I’m sure as sure can be
That the Dinkey-Bird is singing
In the amfalula tree.

For the Dinkey-Bird’s bravuras
And staccatos are so sweet—
His roulades, appoggiaturas,
And robustos so complete,
That the youth of every nation—
Be they near or far away—
Have especial delectation
In that gladsome roundelay.

Their eyes grow bright and brighter
Their lungs begin to crow,
Their hearts get light and lighter,
And their cheeks are all aglow;
For an echo cometh bringing
The news to all and me,
That the Dinkey-Bird is singing
In the amfalula tree.

I’m sure you like to go there
To see your feathered friend—
And so many goodies grow there
You would like to comprehend!
Speed, little dreams, your winging
To that land across the sea
Where the Dinkey-Bird is singing
In the amfalula tree!

questions.prompt: Which ordinary fruits are replaced by sweets in Wonder-Wander?
facilitatorNotes: Gumdrops grow like cherries and caramels are picked like berries. Ask what the comparisons let us imagine.
evidence: Caramels you pick like berries

questions.prompt: What does the speaker hear that makes the Dinkey-Bird seem near?
facilitatorNotes: Children laughing and playing. The poem connects real joy with its invented bird song.
evidence: When I hear their laughter ringing

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza invite a journey without giving a real travel route?
facilitatorNotes: It asks little dreams to fly to the land. This signals imaginative travel rather than a place found on a map.
evidence: Speed, little dreams, your winging

days.title: The Fox and the Lion
days.challenge: Track three meetings and compare the fox’s distance and speech.
days.focus: Repetition with a change shows fear giving way to familiarity.
days.context: This is an imaginary animal fable. Its final proverb uses contempt to mean a lack of respect; readers can decide whether that fully describes the fox’s behavior.

excerpt.locator: The Fox and the Lion; begins 'The Fox and the Lion'; ends 'Familiarity breeds contempt.'. Source block range 157–159 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: The Fox and the Lion

When first the Fox saw the Lion he was terribly frightened, and ran away and hid himself in the wood. Next time however he came near the King of Beasts he stopped at a safe distance and watched him pass by. The third time they came near one another the Fox went straight up to the Lion and passed the time of day with him, asking him how his family were, and when he should have the pleasure of seeing him again; then turning his tail, he parted from the Lion without much ceremony.
Familiarity breeds contempt.

questions.prompt: What does the fox do at the first meeting?
facilitatorNotes: He runs away and hides. Ask the child to show the distance with two fingers.
evidence: ran away and hid himself in the wood

questions.prompt: How is the second meeting different from the third?
facilitatorNotes: At the second he watches from a safe distance; at the third he walks up and chats.
evidence: stopped at a safe distance

questions.prompt: Does the lion do anything in the story that explains this new boldness?
facilitatorNotes: No change in the lion is described; repeated encounters change the fox. Discuss whether familiarity must always become disrespect, as the final saying suggests.
evidence: without much ceremony

days.title: Why the Magpie’s Nest Is Not Well Built
days.challenge: Distinguish an offered lesson from a character’s hidden plan.
days.focus: A talking-bird tale connects learning, participation, and an imagined origin.
days.context: Read this as Holbrook’s historical literary adaptation, not a factual lesson about magpie nests. Its imagined conversations invite discussion about joining a task.
days.contentNote: The opening generalizes Indigenous homes using the historical terms Indian and wigwam. Explain that Indigenous peoples have many distinct cultures and homes; the adaptation is not reliable cultural or scientific evidence.

excerpt.locator: Why the Magpie’s Nest Is Not Well Built; begins "WHY THE MAGPIE'S NEST IS NOT WELL BUILT."; ends "and they were busy taking care of them, and had no time to teach the lazy magpie. This is why the magpie's nest is not well built.". Source block range 133–150 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: WHY THE MAGPIE'S NEST IS NOT WELL BUILT.
A long time ago all the birds met together to talk about building nests.
"Every Indian has a wigwam," said the robin, "and every bird needs a home."
"Indians have no feathers," said the owl, "and so they are cold without wigwams. We have feathers."
"I keep warm by flying swiftly," said the swallow.
"And I keep warm by fluttering my wings," said the humming-bird.

"By and by we shall have our little ones," said the robin. "They will have no feathers on their wings, so they cannot fly or flutter; and they will be cold. How shall we keep them warm if we have no nests?"
Then all the birds said, "We will build nests so that our little ones will be warm."

The birds went to work. One brought twigs, one brought moss, and one brought leaves. They sang together merrily, for they thought of the little ones that would some time come to live in the warm nests.
Now the magpie was lazy, and she sat still and watched the others at their work.
"Come and build your nest in the reeds and rushes," cried one bird, but the magpie said "No."
"My nest is on the branch of a tree," called another, "and it rocks like a child's cradle. Come and build beside it," but the magpie said "No."
Before long all the birds but the magpie had their nests built. The magpie cried, "I do not know how to build a nest. Will you not help me?"

The other birds were sorry for her and answered, "We will teach you." The black-bird said, "Put the twigs on this bough;" the robin said, "Put the leaves between the twigs;" and the humming-bird said, "Put this soft green moss over it all."
"I do not know how," cried the magpie.
"We are teaching you," said the other birds. But the magpie was lazy, and she thought, "If I do not learn, they will build a nest for me."
The other birds talked together. "She does not wish to learn," they said, "and we will not help her any longer." So they went away from her.

Then the magpie was sorry. "Come back," she called, "and I will learn." But by this time the other birds had eggs in their nests, and they were busy taking care of them, and had no time to teach the lazy magpie. This is why the magpie's nest is not well built.

questions.prompt: Why does the robin say the birds need nests even though adults have feathers?
facilitatorNotes: Their young cannot yet fly or flutter to keep warm, in the story’s explanation.
evidence: They will have no feathers on their wings

questions.prompt: What does the magpie privately hope will happen if she does not learn?
facilitatorNotes: She expects the other birds to build for her. This differs from simply finding a new skill difficult.
evidence: If I do not learn, they will build a nest for me.

questions.prompt: Why are the other birds unable to return when the magpie finally offers to learn?
facilitatorNotes: They now have eggs to care for. Discuss this particular timing, without saying learners who struggle should lose help.
evidence: they were busy taking care of them

days.title: The Humming-Top
days.challenge: Notice when a poem moves from a child’s present play to an adult’s memory.
days.focus: Sound words animate a toy while the final questions add a wistful feeling.
days.context: A top is an old spinning toy. Read the archaic verb endings naturally, then reread a few sound-rich lines. The poem’s play instructions are part of its historical scene.

excerpt.locator:
The Humming-Top; begins 'THE HUMMING-TOP'; ends ' ever this toy
Of my dear little boy,
When the years have worn away,
Sing sad and low
Of the long ago,
As it singeth to me to-day?'. Source block range 473–476 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: THE HUMMING-TOP

The top it hummeth a sweet, sweet song
To my dear little boy at play—
Merrily singeth all day long,
As it spinneth and spinneth away.
And my dear little boy
He laugheth with joy
When he heareth the monotone
Of that busy thing
That loveth to sing
The song that is all its own.

Hold fast the string and wind it tight,
That the song be loud and clear;
Now hurl the top with all your might
Upon the banquette here;
And straight from the string
The joyous thing
Boundeth and spinneth along,
And it whirrs and it chirrs
And it birrs and it purrs
Ever its pretty song.

Will ever my dear little boy grow old,
As some have grown before?
Will ever his heart feel faint and cold,
When he heareth the songs of yore?
Will ever this toy
Of my dear little boy,
When the years have worn away,
Sing sad and low
Of the long ago,
As it singeth to me to-day?

questions.prompt: Which words make the spinning toy seem to sing?
facilitatorNotes: Hummeth, whirrs, chirrs, birrs, and purrs create sound. Invite the child to imitate two and compare.
evidence: And it whirrs and it chirrs

questions.prompt: Who enjoys the top in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The little boy laughs with joy. Later the adult’s questions add a different feeling.
evidence: He laugheth with joy

questions.prompt: Why does the final stanza ask about the boy growing old?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker imagines that the toy may one day bring memories, as it does for the speaker now. Accept thoughtful uncertainty about the future.
evidence: As it singeth to me to-day?

days.title: The Wilful Little Breeze — away from home
days.challenge: Trace how the same setting changes from play to loneliness as daylight fades.
days.focus: Personified weather encounters a hidden danger and a chance to help.
days.context: Part 1 of a chapter continued tomorrow. The Breezes are imaginary children of the wind, not a scientific explanation.
days.contentNote: A childlike Breeze is lonely at night and hears predators planning to eat birds. The next part resolves the danger with every Bob White safely moved.

excerpt.locator: The Wilful Little Breeze — away from home; begins 'OLD MOTHER WEST WIND was tired—tired and just a wee bit cross—cross because she was tired. She had h'; ends 'ites that very minute. It made the wilful little Breeze shiver to see them. Pretty soon they started on towards the Brown Pasture.'. Source block range 112–121 in the documented transcription extraction. Dated 1914 witness printed pages 41–44.

blocks.text: OLD MOTHER WEST WIND was tired—tired and just a wee bit cross—cross because she was tired. She had had a very busy day. Ever since early morning she had been puffing out the white sails of the ships on the big ocean that they might go faster; she had kept all the big and little wind mills whirling and whirling to pump water for thirsty folks and grind corn for hungry folks; she had blown away all the smoke from tall chimneys and engines and steamboats. Yes, indeed, Old Mother West Wind had been very, very busy.

Now she was coming across the Green Meadows on her way to her home behind the Purple Hills, and as she came she opened the big bag she carried and called to her children, the Merry Little Breezes, who had been playing hard on the Green Meadows all the long day. One by one they crept into the big bag, for they were tired, too, and ready to go to their home behind the Purple Hills.

Pretty soon all were in the bag but one, a wilful little Breeze, who was not quite ready to go home; he wanted to play just a little longer. He danced ahead of Old Mother West Wind. He kissed the sleepy daisies. He shook the nodding buttercups. He set all the little poplar leaves a dancing, too, and he wouldn’t come into the big bag.
So Old Mother West Wind closed the big bag and slung it over her shoulder. Then she started on towards her home behind the Purple Hills.

When she had gone the wilful little Breeze left behind suddenly felt very lonely—very lonely indeed! The sleepy daisies didn’t want to play. The nodding buttercups were cross. Great round bright Mr. Sun, who had been shining and shining all day long, went to bed and put on his night cap of golden clouds. Black shadows came creeping, creeping out into the Green Meadows.
The wilful little Breeze began to wish that he was safe in Old Mother West Wind’s big bag with all the other Merry Little Breezes.

So he started across the Green Meadows to find the Purple Hills. But all the hills were black now and he could not tell which he should look behind to find his home with Old Mother West Wind and the Merry Little Breezes. How he did wish that he had minded Old Mother West Wind.

By and by he curled up under a bayberry bush and tried to go to sleep, but he was lonely, oh, so lonely! and he couldn’t go to sleep. Old Mother Moon came up and flooded all the Green Meadows with light, but it wasn’t like the bright light of jolly round Mr. Sun, for it was cold and white and it made many black shadows.

Pretty soon the wilful little Breeze heard Hooty the Owl out hunting for a meadow mouse for his dinner. Then down the Lone Little Path which ran close to the bayberry bush trotted Reddy Fox. He was trotting very softly and every minute or so he turned his head and looked behind him to see if he was followed. It was plain to see that Reddy Fox was bent on mischief.

When he reached the bayberry bush Reddy Fox sat down and barked twice. Hooty the Owl answered him at once and flew over to join him. They didn’t see the wilful little Breeze curled up under the bayberry bush, so intent were these two rogues in plotting mischief. They were planning to steal down across the Green Meadows to the edge of the Brown Pasture where Mr. Bob White and pretty Mrs. Bob White and a dozen little Bob Whites had their home.

“When they run along the ground I’ll catch ’em, and when they fly up in the air you’ll catch ’em and we’ll gobble ’em all up,” said Reddy Fox to Hooty the Owl. Then he licked his chops and Hooty the Owl snapped his bill, just as if they were tasting tender little Bob Whites that very minute. It made the wilful little Breeze shiver to see them. Pretty soon they started on towards the Brown Pasture.

questions.prompt: Why is Old Mother West Wind tired rather than simply in a bad mood?
facilitatorNotes: She has spent the day moving ships, turning mills, and clearing smoke. The opening connects work and fatigue.
evidence: cross because she was tired

questions.prompt: What changes for the little Breeze after the others leave?
facilitatorNotes: The flowers no longer want to play and darkness makes the hills hard to identify.
evidence: he could not tell which he should look behind

questions.prompt: What do the Breeze’s hiding place and overheard conversation make possible?
facilitatorNotes: He hears the Fox and Owl plan to catch the Bob Whites. Discuss what useful action that knowledge might allow, while keeping it a prediction.
evidence: They didn’t see the wilful little Breeze

days.title: The Wilful Little Breeze — a warning in time
days.challenge: Follow how knowledge from the earlier scene leads to a successful rescue.
days.focus: Speed, a shorter route, and a quiet warning reverse the predators’ plan.
days.context: Part 2 and the end of the chapter. The Breeze has overheard a plan to catch the Bob White family and now rushes to warn them.
days.contentNote: The predators spring at an empty sleeping place. The birds remain safe; none is caught.

excerpt.locator: The Wilful Little Breeze — a warning in time; begins 'When they were out of sight the wilful little Breeze jumped up and shook himself. Then away he sped '; ends 'lful little Breeze went back to the juniper tree and curled himself up beside Mr. Bob White to sleep, for he was lonely no longer.'. Source block range 122–129 in the documented transcription extraction. Dated 1914 witness printed pages 45–46.

blocks.text: When they were out of sight the wilful little Breeze jumped up and shook himself. Then away he sped across the Green Meadows to the Brown Pasture. And because he could go faster and because he went a shorter way he got there first. He had to hunt and hunt to find Mrs. and Mr. Bob White and all the little Bob Whites, but finally he did find them, all with their heads tucked under their wings fast asleep.
The wilful little Breeze shook Mr. Bob White very gently. In an instant he was wide awake.
“Sh-h-h,” said the wilful little Breeze. “Reddy Fox and Hooty the Owl are coming to the Brown Pasture to gobble up you and Mrs. Bob White and all the little Bob Whites.”
“Thank you, little Breeze,” said Mr. Bob White, “I think I’ll move my family.”

Then he woke Mrs. Bob White and all the little Bob Whites. With Mr. Bob White in the lead away they all flew to the far side of the Brown Pasture where they were soon safely hidden under a juniper tree.

The wilful little Breeze saw them safely there, and when they were nicely hidden hurried back to the place where the Bob Whites had been sleeping. Reddy Fox was stealing up through the grass very, very softly. Hooty the Owl was flying as silently as a shadow. When Reddy Fox thought he was near enough he drew himself together, made a quick spring and landed right in Mr. Bob White’s empty bed. Reddy Fox and Hooty the Owl looked so surprised and foolish when they found that the Bob Whites were not there that the wilful little Breeze nearly laughed out loud.
Then Reddy Fox and Hooty the Owl hunted here and hunted there, all over the Brown Pasture, but they couldn’t find the Bob Whites.
And the wilful little Breeze went back to the juniper tree and curled himself up beside Mr. Bob White to sleep, for he was lonely no longer.

questions.prompt: How does the Breeze reach the birds before the Fox and Owl?
facilitatorNotes: He travels faster and takes a shorter way.
evidence: because he went a shorter way he got there first

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Bob White do instead of arguing about the warning?
facilitatorNotes: He thanks the Breeze and moves his family to a hidden place.
evidence: I think I’ll move my family.

questions.prompt: How does the last line change the Breeze’s loneliness from the first part?
facilitatorNotes: He sleeps beside the bird family after helping them and is lonely no longer. Connect companionship with his action, not only with a change of location.
evidence: for he was lonely no longer

blocks.text: PUPPY AND I

I met a man as I went walking;
We got talking,
Man and I.
“Where are you going to, Man?” I said

“Down to the village, to get some bread.
Will you come with me?” “No, not I.”

I met a Horse as I went walking;
We got talking,
Horse and I.
“Where are you going to, Horse, to-day?”
(I said to the Horse as he went by).
“Down to the village to get some hay.
Will you come with me?” “No, not I.”

I met a Woman as I went walking;
We got talking,
Woman and I.
“Where are you going to, Woman, so early?”
(I said to the Woman as she went by).
“Down to the village to get some barley.
Will you come with me?” “No, not I.”

I met some Rabbits as I went walking;
We got talking,
Rabbits and I.
“Where are you going in your brown fur coats?”
(I said to the Rabbits as they went by.
“Down to the village to get some oats.
Will you come with us?” “No, not I.”

I met a Puppy as I went walking;
We got talking,
Puppy and I.
“Where are you going this nice fine day?”

days.title: Mrs. Tabby Gray
days.challenge: Follow what the reader knows that the helpful human does not yet understand.
days.focus: A mother cat persists until another character recognizes the real problem.
days.context: The complete story follows a cat’s attempted move, excluding the separate adult teaching motto. Cats are given human-like thoughts and speech.
days.contentNote: A kitten is accidentally shut in a trunk and then promptly found unharmed. This is a historical story, not advice about animal food or housing.

excerpt.locator: Mrs. Tabby Gray; begins 'Mrs. Tabby Gray, with her three little kittens, lived out in the barn where the hay was stored. One '; ends 'And she never afterwards changed her mind.'. Source block range 55–72 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: Mrs. Tabby Gray, with her three little kittens, lived out in the barn where the hay was stored. One of the kittens was white, one was black, and one gray, just like her mother, who was called Tabby Gray from the color of her coat.

These three little kittens opened their eyes when they grew old enough, and thought there was nothing so nice in all this wonderful world as their own dear mother, although she told them of a great many nice things, like milk and bread, which they should have when they could go up to the big house where she had her breakfast, dinner, and supper.

Every time Mother Tabby came from the big house she had something pleasant to tell. "Bones for dinner to-day, my dears," she would say, or "I had a fine romp with a ball and the baby," until the kittens longed for the time when they could go too.
One day, however, Mother Cat walked in with joyful news.
"I have found an elegant new home for you," she said, "in a very large trunk where some old clothes are kept; and I think I had better move at once."
Then she picked up the small black kitten, without any more words, and walked right out of the barn with him.
The black kitten was astonished, but he blinked his eyes at the bright sunshine, and tried to see everything.

Out in the barnyard there was a great noise, for the white hen had laid an egg, and wanted everybody to know it; but Mother Cat hurried on, without stopping to inquire about it, and soon dropped the kitten into the large trunk. The clothes made such a soft, comfortable bed, and the kitten was so tired after his exciting trip, that he fell asleep, and Mrs. Tabby trotted off for another baby.

While she was away, the lady who owned the trunk came out in the hall; and when she saw that the trunk was open, she shut it, locked it, and put the key in her pocket, for she did not dream that there was anything so precious as a kitten inside.

As soon as the lady had gone upstairs Mrs. Tabby Gray came back, with the little white kitten; and when she found the trunk closed, she was terribly frightened. She put the white kitten down and sprang on top of the trunk and scratched with all her might, but scratching did no good. Then she jumped down and reached up to the keyhole, but that was too small for even a mouse to pass through, and the poor mother mewed pitifully.

What was she to do? She picked up the white kitten, and ran to the barn with it. Then she made haste to the house again, and went upstairs to the lady's room. The lady was playing with her baby and when Mother Cat saw this she rubbed against her skirts, and cried: "Mee-ow, mee-ow! You have your baby, and I want mine! Mee-ow, mee-ow!"

By and by the lady said: "Poor Kitty! she must be hungry"; and she went down to the kitchen and poured sweet milk in a saucer, but the cat did not want milk. She wanted her baby kitten out of the big black trunk, and she mewed as plainly as she could: "Give me my baby—give me my baby, out of your big black trunk!"

The kind lady decided that she must be thirsty: "Poor Kitty, I will give you water"; but when she set the bowl of water down Mrs. Tabby Gray mewed more sorrowfully than before. She wanted no water,—she only wanted her dear baby kitten; and she ran to and fro, crying, until, at last, the lady followed her; and she led the way to the trunk.

"What can be the matter with this cat?" said the lady; and she took the trunk key out of her pocket, put it in the lock, unlocked the trunk, raised the top—and in jumped Mother Cat with such a bound that the little black kitten waked up with a start.

"Purr, purr, my darling child," said Mrs. Tabby Gray, in great excitement; "I have had a dreadful fright!" and before the black kitten could ask one question she picked him up and started for the barn.

The sun was bright in the barnyard and the hens were still chattering there; but the black kitten was glad to get back to the barn. His mother was glad, too; for, as she nestled down in the hay with her three little kittens, she told them that a barn was the best place after all to raise children.
And she never afterwards changed her mind.

questions.prompt: Why does the lady lock the trunk without realizing she is causing trouble?
facilitatorNotes: She does not know a kitten is sleeping inside. The reader has seen it placed there.
evidence: she did not dream that there was anything so precious as a kitten inside

questions.prompt: Why do milk and water fail to answer the cat’s cries?
facilitatorNotes: The cat wants her kitten, not food or drink. Compare the lady’s guesses with the reader’s knowledge.
evidence: she only wanted her dear baby kitten

questions.prompt: What finally helps the lady understand enough to act?
facilitatorNotes: She follows the cat to the trunk and opens it. Discuss the value of watching actions as well as making guesses.
evidence: the lady followed her; and she led the way to the trunk

days.title: The Two Crabs
days.challenge: Hear the difference between giving an instruction and demonstrating it.
days.focus: A brief reply turns a parent’s criticism into a request for an example.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator: The Two Crabs; begins 'The Two Crabs'; ends 'Example is the best precept.'. Source block range 208–211 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: The Two Crabs

One fine day two Crabs came out from their home to take a stroll on the sand. “Child,” said the mother, “you are walking very ungracefully. You should accustom yourself, to walking straight forward without twisting from side to side.”
“Pray, mother,” said the young one, “do but set the example yourself, and I will follow you.”
Example is the best precept.

questions.prompt: What change in walking does the mother request?
facilitatorNotes: She wants the young crab to move straight forward rather than side to side.
evidence: without twisting from side to side

questions.prompt: Does the young crab simply refuse to try?
facilitatorNotes: No; it asks the mother to show the requested movement and promises to follow.
evidence: do but set the example yourself

questions.prompt: How does the final saying fit this exchange?
facilitatorNotes: Showing a behavior can teach more clearly than telling. Ask for a familiar skill where a demonstration helps; do not assume the story proves all advice is useless.
evidence: Example is the best precept.

days.title: Why the Evergreen Trees Never Lose Their Leaves
days.challenge: Compare several refusals with three different forms of help.
days.focus: A nature myth personifies trees and rewards their treatment of a vulnerable bird.
days.context: A historical literary adaptation about speaking trees. Read for the contrasting choices and kindness; real evergreen behavior is not caused by a frost king.
days.contentNote: The bird is injured but receives shelter and food. The trees’ judgments are imaginary character choices, not facts about particular kinds of trees.

excerpt.locator: Why the Evergreen Trees Never Lose Their Leaves; begins 'WHY THE EVERGREEN TREES NEVER LOSE THEIR LEAVES.'; ends 'This is why the leaves of the spruce, the pine, and the juniper are always green.'. Source block range 566–589 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: WHY THE EVERGREEN TREES NEVER LOSE THEIR LEAVES.

Winter was coming, and the birds had flown far to the south, where the air was warm and they could find berries to eat. One little bird had broken its wing and could not fly with the others. It was alone in the cold world of frost and snow. The forest looked warm, and it made its way to the trees as well as it could, to ask for help.
First it came to a birch-tree. "Beautiful birch-tree," it said, "my wing is broken, and my friends have flown away. May I live among your branches till they come back to me?"
"No, indeed," answered the birch-tree, drawing her fair green leaves away. "We of the great forest have our own birds to help. I can do nothing for you."

"The birch is not very strong," said the little bird to itself, "and it might be that she could not hold me easily. I will ask the oak." So the bird said, "Great oak-tree, you are so strong, will you not let me live on your boughs till my friends come back in the springtime?"

"In the springtime!" cried the oak. "That is a long way off. How do I know what you might do in all that time? Birds are always looking for something to eat, and you might even eat up some of my acorns."

"It may be that the willow will be kind to me," thought the bird, and it said, "Gentle willow, my wing is broken, and I could not fly to the south with the other birds. May I live on your branches till the springtime?"

The willow did not look gentle then, for she drew herself up proudly and said, "Indeed, I do not know you, and we willows never talk to people whom we do not know. Very likely there are trees somewhere that will take in strange birds. Leave me at once."

The poor little bird did not know what to do. Its wing was not yet strong, but it began to fly away as well as it could. Before it had gone far, a voice was heard. "Little bird," it said, "where are you going?"
"Indeed, I do not know," answered the bird sadly. "I am very cold."
"Come right here, then," said the friendly spruce-tree, for it was her voice that had called. "You shall live on my warmest branch all winter if you choose."
"Will you really let me?" asked the little bird eagerly.
"Indeed, I will," answered the kind-hearted spruce-tree. "If your friends have flown away, it is time for the trees to help you. Here is the branch where my leaves are thickest and softest."
"My branches are not very thick," said the friendly pine-tree, "but I am big and strong, and I can keep the north wind from you and the spruce."
"I can help too," said a little juniper-tree. "I can give you berries all winter long, and every bird knows that juniper berries are good."
So the spruce gave the lonely little bird a home, the pine kept the cold north wind away from it, and the juniper gave it berries to eat.
The other trees looked on and talked together wisely.
"I would not have strange birds on my boughs," said the birch.
"I shall not give my acorns away for any one," said the oak.
"I never have anything to do with strangers," said the willow, and the three trees drew their leaves closely about them.
In the morning all those shining green leaves lay on the ground, for a cold north wind had come in the night, and every leaf that it touched fell from the tree.
"May I touch every leaf in the forest?" asked the wind in its frolic.
"No," said the frost king. "The trees that have been kind to the little bird with the broken wing may keep their leaves."
This is why the leaves of the spruce, the pine, and the juniper are always green.

questions.prompt: Why can this bird not leave with the others?
facilitatorNotes: Its wing is broken, so it cannot make their journey south.
evidence: One little bird had broken its wing

questions.prompt: How do the spruce, pine, and juniper divide the helping work?
facilitatorNotes: Spruce gives shelter, pine blocks wind, and juniper gives berries. Have the child connect each tree to its gift.
evidence: the juniper gave it berries to eat

questions.prompt: What imagined explanation does the ending give for green leaves in winter?
facilitatorNotes: The frost king spares the helpful trees’ leaves. Explain that this is the story’s moral fantasy, not botanical evidence.
evidence: may keep their leaves

days.title: The Ride to Bumpville
days.challenge: Keep the opening pretend frame in mind during increasingly wild travel language.
days.focus: Rhythm turns an adult’s knee into a comic galloping ride.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator:
The Ride to Bumpville; begins 'THE RIDE TO BUMPVILLE'; ends 'int,
The calico mare must be blowing and faint—
What’s more to the point, I’m blowed if I ain’t!
So play we have got to Bumpville!'. Source block range 483–488 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: THE RIDE TO BUMPVILLE

Play that my knee was a calico mare
Saddled and bridled for Bumpville;
Leap to the back of this steed, if you dare,
And gallop away to Bumpville!
I hope you’ll be sure to sit fast in your seat,
For this calico mare is prodigiously fleet,
And many adventures you’re likely to meet
As you journey along to Bumpville.

This calico mare both gallops and trots
While whisking you off to Bumpville;
She paces, she shies, and she stumbles, in spots,
In the tortuous road to Bumpville;
And sometimes this strangely mercurial steed
Will suddenly stop and refuse to proceed,
Which, all will admit, is vexatious indeed,
When one is en route to Bumpville!

She’s scared of the cars when the engine goes “Toot!”
Down by the crossing at Bumpville;
You’d better look out for that treacherous brute
Bearing you off to Bumpville!
With a snort she rears up on her hindermost heels,
And executes jigs and Virginia reels—
Words fail to explain how embarrassed one feels
Dancing so wildly to Bumpville!

It’s bumpytybump and it’s jiggytyjog,
Journeying on to Bumpville;
It’s over the hilltop and down through the bog
You ride on your way to Bumpville;
It’s rattletybang over boulder and stump,
There are rivers to ford, there are fences to jump,
And the corduroy road it goes bumpytybump,
Mile after mile to Bumpville!

Perhaps you’ll observe it’s no easy thing
Making the journey to Bumpville,
So I think, on the whole, it were prudent to bring
An end to this ride to Bumpville;
For, though she has uttered no protest or plaint,
The calico mare must be blowing and faint—
What’s more to the point, I’m blowed if I ain’t!
So play we have got to Bumpville!

questions.prompt: What is the calico mare really at the beginning?
facilitatorNotes: The adult’s knee in a pretend game. This frame explains the bumpy journey that follows.
evidence: Play that my knee was a calico mare

questions.prompt: Which made-up sound words help you hear the ride?
facilitatorNotes: Bumpytybump, jiggytyjog, and rattletybang fit. Ask how their repeated beats imitate jolting movement.
evidence: It’s bumpytybump and it’s jiggytyjog

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker decide they have arrived at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The pretend horse and the adult giving the ride are tired. The last joke brings us back to the real play.
evidence: I’m blowed if I ain’t!

days.title: How the Home Was Built — a family plan
days.challenge: Keep track of a shared goal while different family members work in different places.
days.focus: A cumulative home-building story connects visible construction with less visible care.
days.context: A historical family story, not a rule about which family member must do which job. The family already lives in a rented home; it hopes to own a house together.

excerpt.locator: How the Home Was Built — a family plan; begins 'Once there was a very dear family,—Father, Mother, big Brother Tom, little Sister Polly, and the bab'; ends 'stored away the firewood and put up the stoves; and when the wood-choppers went to the great forest, he was ready to go with them.'. Source block range 190–204 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: Once there was a very dear family,—Father, Mother, big Brother Tom, little Sister Polly, and the baby, who had a very long name, Gustavus Adolphus; and every one of the family wanted a home more than anything else in the world.

They lived in a house, of course, but that was rented; and they wanted a home of their very own, with a sunny room for Mother and Father and Baby, with a wee room close by for the little sister; a big, airy room for Brother Tom; a cosy room for the cooking and eating; and, best of all, a room that Grandmother might call her own when she came to see them.
A box which Tom had made always stood on Mother's mantel, and they called it the "Home Bank," because every penny that could be spared was dropped in there for the building of the home.
This box had been full once, and was emptied to buy a little piece of ground where the home could be built when the box was full again.
