days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 8: The Forest Meeting
days.challenge: Use knowledge shared with the listener but not with every character.
days.focus: An unexpected welcome reveals how a person has changed.
days.context: Spare has escaped from court and is searching the forest for his doublet. Scrub and Fairfeather are living in a hut of boughs, and Scrub is wearing the doublet.
days.contentNote: Food is cooked over a fire in the forest.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — The Forest Meeting; begins “"Determined to find his doublet, and sure that neither …” and ends “… his life, though we live in this poor hut.'”.

blocks.text: "Determined to find his doublet, and sure that neither crowd nor courtiers could catch him in the forest, Spare went on his way, and was soon among the tall trees; but neither hut nor dwarf could he see. Moreover, the night came on; the wood was dark and tangled, but here and there the moon shone through its alleys, the great owls flitted about, and the nightingales sang. So he went on, hoping to find some place of shelter. At last the red light of a fire, gleaming through a thicket, led him to the door of a low hut. It stood half open, as if there was nothing to fear, and within he saw his brother Scrub snoring loudly on a bed of grass, at the foot of which lay his own leathern doublet; while Fairfeather, in a kirtle made of plaited rushes, sat roasting pheasants' eggs by the fire.
"'Good evening, mistress,' said Spare, stepping in.
"The blaze shone on him, but so changed was her brother-in-law with his court-life, that Fairfeather did not know him, and she answered far more courteously than was her wont.
"'Good evening, master. Whence come ye so late? but speak low, for my good man has sorely tired himself cleaving wood, and is taking a sleep, as you see, before supper.'
"'A good rest to him,' said Spare, perceiving he was not known. 'I come from the court for a day's hunting, and have lost my way in the forest.'
"'Sit down and have a share of our supper,' said Fairfeather, 'I will put some more eggs in the ashes; and tell me the news of court—I used to think of it long ago when I was young and foolish.'
"'Did you never go there?' said the cobbler. 'So fair a dame as you would make the ladies marvel.'

"'You are pleased to flatter,' said Fairfeather; 'but my husband has a brother there, and we left our moorland village to try our fortune also. An old woman enticed us with fair words and strong drink at the entrance of this forest, where we fell asleep and dreamt of great things; but when we woke, everything had been robbed from us—my looking-glass, my scarlet cloak, my husband's Sunday coat; and, in place of all, the robbers left him that old leathern doublet, which he has worn ever since, and never was so merry in all his life, though we live in this poor hut.'

questions.prompt: What helps Spare find shelter when he cannot see a path to a house?
facilitatorNotes: A red firelight shines through the thicket. The sensory detail turns an uncertain dark journey toward a meeting.
evidence: the red light of a fire, gleaming through a thicket

questions.prompt: Why does Fairfeather not greet Spare as a relative at first?
facilitatorNotes: His life at court has changed his appearance; she does not recognise him. The listener knows more than she does.
evidence: Fairfeather did not know him

questions.prompt: What has changed in Fairfeather’s manner since the wedding that excluded Spare?
facilitatorNotes: She politely invites the stranger to share supper and adds more eggs. This welcome contrasts with her earlier pride.
evidence: Sit down and have a share of our supper

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 9: Home with Three Leaves
days.challenge: Compare a character’s stated fortune with what others expect fortune to mean.
days.focus: A reunion changes the family’s choice of gifts and their everyday work.
days.context: Spare has found his brother and Fairfeather living in a forest hut, with his missing coat. She still does not recognise their guest.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — Home with Three Leaves; begins “"'It is a shabby doublet, that,' said Spare, taking …” and ends “… I last heard the news of the north country."”.

blocks.text: "'It is a shabby doublet, that,' said Spare, taking up the garment, and seeing that it was his own, for the merry leaves were still sewed in its lining. 'It would be good for hunting in, however—your husband would be glad to part with it, I dare say, in exchange for this handsome cloak;' and he pulled off the green mantle and buttoned on the doublet, much to Fairfeather's delight, who ran and shook Scrub, crying—
"'Husband! husband! rise and see what a good bargain I have made.'
"Scrub gave one closing snore, and muttered something about the root being hard; but he rubbed his eyes, gazed up at his brother, and said—
"'Spare, is that really you? How did you like the court, and have you made your fortune?'

"'That I have, brother,' said Spare, 'in getting back my own good leathern doublet. Come, let us eat eggs, and rest ourselves here this night. In the morning we will return to our own old hut, at the end of the moorland village where the Christmas Cuckoo will come and bring us leaves.'

"Scrub and Fairfeather agreed. So in the morning they all returned, and found the old hut little the worse for wear and weather. The neighbours came about them to ask the news of court, and see if they had made their fortune. Everybody was astonished to find the three poorer than ever, but somehow they liked to go back to the hut. Spare brought out the lasts and awls he had hidden in a corner; Scrub and he began their old trade, and the whole north country found out that there never were such cobblers.

"They mended the shoes of lords and ladies as well as the common people; everybody was satisfied. Their custom increased from day to day, and all that were disappointed, discontented, or unlucky, came to the hut as in old times, before Spare went to court.

"The rich brought them presents, the poor did them service. The hut itself changed, no one knew how. Flowering honeysuckle grew over its roof; red and white roses grew thick about its door. Moreover, the Christmas Cuckoo always came on the first of April, bringing three leaves of the merry tree—for Scrub and Fairfeather would have no more golden ones. So it was with them when I last heard the news of the north country."

questions.prompt: Why does Fairfeather think exchanging the coat for Spare’s cloak is an excellent bargain?
facilitatorNotes: The cloak looks rich; she does not know the green leaves are sewn inside the old coat. Different knowledge creates different judgments.
evidence: seeing that it was his own, for the merry leaves were still sewed in its lining

questions.prompt: What does Spare mean when he says he has made his fortune?
facilitatorNotes: He means recovering his own coat, not collecting new money or rank. Ask the child to connect the answer to what the coat contains.
evidence: in getting back my own good leathern doublet

questions.prompt: How do the final three leaves show that Scrub and Fairfeather have changed their minds?
facilitatorNotes: They now choose merry leaves along with Spare instead of gold; the annual gift includes all three.
evidence: Scrub and Fairfeather would have no more golden ones

days.title: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Scarlet Shoes for Snowflower
days.challenge: Move from an embedded story back to its listeners.
days.focus: Different responses reveal what people took from the same tale.
days.context: The chair has just finished the Christmas Cuckoo tale, ending with a happy family in a flowering hut. Snowflower and the royal listeners respond.
days.contentNote: Mentions ale being given to a child, a historical story detail rather than suitable present-day practice.

excerpt.locator: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Scarlet Shoes for Snowflower; begins “"What a summer-house that hut would make for me, …” and ends “… under the cushion, "to the story of Lady Greensleeves."”.

blocks.text: "What a summer-house that hut would make for me, mamma!" said the Princess Greedalind.

"We must have it brought here bodily," said Queen Wantall; but the chair was silent, and a lady and two noble squires, clad in russet-coloured satin and yellow buskins, the like of which had never been seen at that court, rose up and said—
"That's our story."

"I have not heard such a tale," said King Winwealth, "since my brother Wisewit went from me, and was lost in the forest. Redheels, the seventh of my pages, go and bring this little maid a pair of scarlet shoes with golden buckles."

The seventh page immediately brought from the royal store a pair of scarlet satin shoes with buckles of gold. Snowflower never had seen the like before, and joyfully thanking the king, she dropped a courtesy, seated herself and said—"Chair of my grandmother, take me to the worst kitchen." Immediately the chair marched away as it came, to the admiration of that noble company.

The little girl was allowed to sleep on some straw at the kitchen fire that night. Next day they gave her ale with the scraps the cook threw away. The feast went on with great music and splendour, and the people clamoured without; but in the evening King Winwealth again fell into low spirits, and the royal command was told to Snowflower by the chief scullion, that she and her chair should go to the highest banquet hall, for his majesty wished to hear another story.

When Snowflower had washed her face, and dusted her chair, she went up seated as before, only that she had on the scarlet shoes. Queen Wantall and her daughter looked more spiteful than ever, but some of the company graciously noticed Snowflower's courtesy, and were pleased when she laid down her head, saying, "Chair of my grandmother, tell me a story."
"Listen," said the clear voice from under the cushion, "to the story of Lady Greensleeves."

questions.prompt: What does the princess notice about the hut, and how is that different from the family’s enjoyment of it?
facilitatorNotes: She wants it as her own summer-house; the family valued shared life there. The queen even proposes moving it bodily.
evidence: What a summer-house that hut would make for me, mamma!

questions.prompt: What makes the tale seem connected to people in the banquet hall?
facilitatorNotes: Three richly dressed listeners stand and identify it as their story. This moment joins the magical story and its surrounding setting.
evidence: That's our story.

questions.prompt: Do the new shoes immediately change the way the kitchen treats Snowflower?
facilitatorNotes: Only partly, if at all: she still sleeps on straw and receives scraps. The gift is splendid, but equal welcome has not arrived.
evidence: allowed to sleep on some straw at the kitchen fire

days.title: The Mirror
days.challenge: Infer the physical scene from figurative descriptions without an explicit explanation.
days.focus: Quiet repeated words and reflection imagery turn a lake into a mirror.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.

excerpt.locator:
The Mirror; begins 'THE MIRROR'; ends 'e swan in the lake;
And, breast to breast, both motionless,
They waited for the wind’s caress . . .
And all the water was at ease.'. Source block range 224–225 in the documented transcription extraction.

blocks.text: THE MIRROR

Between the woods the afternoon
Is fallen in a golden swoon.
The sun looks down from quiet skies
To where a quiet water lies,
And silent trees stoop down to trees.
And there I saw a white swan make
Another white swan in the lake;
And, breast to breast, both motionless,
They waited for the wind’s caress . . .
And all the water was at ease.

questions.prompt: How can trees seem to stoop down to other trees?
facilitatorNotes: Their reflections appear below them in still water. Invite a second reading to test that explanation.
evidence: silent trees stoop down to trees

questions.prompt: Does a second real swan have to arrive?
facilitatorNotes: No. The water reflects the first swan, making another image.
evidence: Another white swan in the lake

questions.prompt: What would a stronger wind change in this scene?
facilitatorNotes: Ripples would disturb the mirrorlike reflection and stillness. The poem waits for only a gentle caress, so its quiet mood lasts.
evidence: all the water was at ease

days.title: Sand-Between-the-Toes
days.challenge: Track a repeated refrain while listening for new signs of wind in each scene.
days.focus: Sound and personification make a windy beach visit bodily and vivid.
days.context: Listen as an adult reads this original historical text. You may answer aloud and ask to hear a sentence or stanza again.
